newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China cenbank's vow of support for HKMA welcomed.
newsitem.headline: China cenbank's vow of support for HKMA welcomed.

text.p: China's central bank repeated on Wednesday a vow to assist the Hong Kong Monetary Authority in times of financial stress, a move which analysts said reassured local markets.
"With the handover getting closer and closer, to repeat what they have said is a big positive," said Dong Tau, senior regional economist at Schroders Asia Ltd.

"Giving a little moral support and adding weight to the HKMA is probably the primary reason for (the People's Bank of China) to repeat what they have said two dozen times in the last 12 months," said Tau.

People's Bank of China Governor Dai Xianglong was quoted by a Chinese paper as saying that China's central bank would provide assistance to the HKMA if needed in line with market rules and the territory's Basic Law.
"Governer Dai is just reinforcing to the international community that there will be two systems and that the PBOC and the HKMA will keep in close contact," said an HKMA spokesman.
Dai also said that the China's central bank believes that the HKMA is fully capable of handling any volatility in the financial system that may accompany the historic change of sovereignty.

"Even though there may be some fluctuations in Hong Kong's financial markets before and after Beijing resumes sovereignty over the British colony on July 1, we fully believe the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will have the ability to handle the situation," Dai said in a front-page story in the Financial News.
So far, there have been few signs of volatility in Hong Kong markets leading up to the handover of the territory to China after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
In order to guard against chaos in currency markets, Hong Kong and China have signed a bilateral repurchase agreement to come to the aid of each other in times of market stress.
The pact is one of many bilateral agreements signed between Asian countries to help maintain currency stability.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority was tested last month after a hugely oversubscribed initial public offering for red chip Beijing Enterprises put strains on its settlement system.
The issue was more than 1,276 times oversubscribed, locking up an estimated HK$215 billion ($27.8 billion) in subscription money and temporarily driving overnight interest rates sharply higher.
Some analysts have expressed concern that such wildly oversubscribed issues could put strains on the monetary system in future.

But Mike Powell, deputy treasurer and head of interest rates at HSBC Markets, said the problems associated with the settlement of massive initial public offerings were technical in nature and would never require the help of China's central bank.
The HKMA is working on ways to improve the system.
"We've been thinking about what we can do in terms of getting a new mechanism," a source at the HKMA said on Wednesday.

Andrew Fung, head of capital markets at the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said China's central bank already has helped the HKMA in its bid to develop the territory's financial markets by proposing to set up an office in Hong Kong to handle the mainland's foreign currency reserves.
"To have part of their team in Hong Kong to manage some of their reserves is more visible support and gives the banks in Hong Kong more confidence," said Fung.
"This move will help Hong Kong to continue to be one of the major foreign exchange trading centres in Asia," he added.
China's Dai also said that he did not exect Shanghai to replace Hong Kong as a financial centre in the near term.
